newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - As miners rage, gold extends its slide.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - As miners rage, gold extends its slide.

text.p: New shock waves hit gold on Monday from the disclosure last week that Australia had sold bullion from state reserves, and in South Africa one mine is already being shut because the price has dropped so far.
The price collapse to 12-year lows below $320 an ounce - down some $50 since January - fuelled anger in the mining industry along with rising anxiety for the future of some mines.

South Africa's East Rand Proprietary Mines said it would halt work at its Benoni Gold Mining Co Ltd as soon as possible and put it on a care and maintenance basis, because of the low price and losses at the mine. East Rand is a unit of Randgold and Exploration Co Ltd
Gold was fixed in London on Monday at $318.75, its lowest since December 1985 and down from Friday's London close at $324.50.
"It would take a Martian to be bullish at this point," said Andy Smith, precious metals analyst at Union Bank of Switzerland.
The sale of 167 tonnes of gold by the Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) followed disposals earlier in the 1990s by the Belgian and Dutch central banks.
It stampeded already-jittery investors into a sell-off, for fear that more of the 35,000 tonnes of gold owned by institutions may be unloaded in future.

The sale cleaned 60 percent of RBA gold from the vaults and sent an especially bearish signal to the market because Australia is the third largest producer - at 289 tonnes last year - after South Africa and the United States.
Bullion dealers expect investor selling to step up this week. The U.S. Independence Day holiday last Friday may have only postponed some of the unloading, they said.
"Expect an orgy of selling over the next few weeks," one dealer said, adding that he felt this way despite a previous view that the price was about as low as it could get this time round.
"Now we might go to under $300 but if we do, mortgage your house and get into the market," he said.
In industry reactions, Australian gold miners pressed the World Gold Council (WGC), a producer lobby group, to make a statement criticising the action of their country's central bank.
The WGC expressed deep concern, saying that the sale seemed to be "motivated by narrow financial considerations."
"For a leading gold producer to take unnecessary actions that prejudice the well being of a key sector of its economy suggests a lack of sensitivity to the factors impacting the market," it declared.

WGC chief executive officer E. M. Hood said the weak price would put additional pressure on member companies, several of which were in the council's hardship category even before the latest price slide.
"We expect others to follow with prices at these levels," he said.
Stockbroker T. Hoare and Co's mining equities analyst, Roger Chaplin, calculates that many gold miners are already suffering at prices around $320.
Yet some dealers see the market's likely downside target as far down as the 1985 low of $287.25 which they say could be reached shortly.

Gold sank 12 years ago in tandem with a collapse in the price of oil. It had tracked oil higher, to reach a record $850 an ounce early in 1980, at a time when it was seen as an investor refuge from the inflation that had been triggered by the OPEC oil "shocks" of the 1970s.
Chaplin said the average total costs of mining gold were around $350 including head office, exploration, depreciation and financing charges.
In South Africa the cost would be about $334.00, he said.
He said forward sales hedging programmes which had allowed the mines to lock in previous higher prices would help them for now.

The average hedge price received during the first quarter of 1997 was "close to $400 per ounce," Chaplin said. Nevertheless, of the top 11 North American mining companies "five or six will be on the border at today's prices."
"We won't see closures just yet because the forward sales (hedge) contracts are still at a decent price," he said.
However, raising financing for new mines could be a problem, given that the cash cost for a new mine would have to be under $220 an ounce to make it profitable, he said.
"A $250 cash-cost mine is now very marginal," Chaplin said.
New mine financing was also caught in the dilemma that mine reserves and "resources" - reserves of ore not yet fully drilled and proven - had to be reduced lowering the worth of the mine.
What would be profitably mined at a higher price would no longer be economic at current or lower prices and could affect around 20 percent of a mine's resources, he explained.
"At a price of $300 for six months, how much of the South African industry has to close?" he asked.
